messages.body_plain:
Small clarifications:
inla.finn is an internal function that does whatever I needed at a particular point in time, which happened to be visualisation of the reorderings and calculating samples. Currently it is also used internally by inla.spde.sample, which is the function you should call if you want a sample, since inla.finn may change without warning. The function, inla.finn calls the inla program, which calculates a reordering as well as a sample (so it is not calculated in R), and the sample is returned in the same order as the original precision matrix.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I am interested in using the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model on INLA. I would like to know if you have some examples of how to fit that model and extract the parameters.
In my case, I am interested on using it for phylogenetic analyses, that is: a graph with binary bifurcations and variable distances between the nodes, variables are only observed on the terminal nodes. The idea is to model the change of the variable over the graph allowing for different sections of the graph to have different rate of change and possibly direction of change.
I hope I have explained my self. A ref with a brief explanation of this is http://www2.hawaii.edu/~mbutler/PDFs/ButlerKing04.pdf

Look forward for your help and thanks very much in advance.
Best,

Inti Pedroso

messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 2012-02-09 at 10:05 -0800, inti pedroso wrote:
> Hi all,
> I am interested in using the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model on INLA. I would
> like to know if you have some examples of how to fit that model and
> extract the parameters.
> In my case, I am interested on using it for phylogenetic analyses,
> that is: a graph with binary bifurcations and variable distances
> between the nodes, variables are only observed on the terminal nodes.
> The idea is to model the change of the variable over the graph
> allowing for different sections of the graph to have different rate of
> change and possibly direction of change.
> I hope I have explained my self. A ref with a brief explanation of
> this is http://www2.hawaii.edu/~mbutler/PDFs/ButlerKing04.pdf

This topic has been discussed in a post by
Julia Palacios from 27.january.  I don't know if Finn or Dan has some
updates on this issue.

Anyway, you can use of the random-walk models, rw1 or rw2 (or crw2)
which is defined for irregular locations. Since the 'locations' is a bit
confusing sometimes, I've added a small example.

ps1: note that the prior for the rw-models is defined in an absolute
scale, with a typical distance between the locations of 1. so if you
scale the 'time' you need to change the prior.

ps2: if you have two locations to close, there can be a numerical
singularity and you  get an error...

****************************

n = 100
interval = c(1, n)
x = seq(interval[1], interval[2],  len = n)
ff = splinefun(x, sin(x/n * 4*pi))

## in the first case, we will have observations for all locations in the
## rw2 model at irregular locations

observation.locations = sort(runif(n, min=interval[1], max=interval[2]))
y = ff(observation.locations) + rnorm(n, sd=0.01)
r1 = inla(y ~ -1 + f(observation.locations, model="rw2", constr=FALSE),
        data = data.frame(y, observation.locations))

## in the second case, we want to estimate the rw2 model with higher
## resultion, but we only have observations at
## 'observations.locations'. hence, we add the locations 1:n,
## additionally, to the rw2 model. this is done using the argument
## 'values'.

## these are the 'locations' for the rw2 model
values = unique(sort(c(1:n, observation.locations)))

## we need to pass these locations as argument 'values', otherwise,
## they are determined by the 'observation.locations' argument.

r2 = inla(y ~ -1 +
        f(observation.locations, model="rw2",
          values=values, constr=FALSE),
        data = list(y=y, observation.locations=observation.locations,
                values=values))

plot(r2$summary.random$observation.locations$ID,
     r2$summary.random$observation.locations$mean, pch=1)
points(r1$summary.random$observation.locations$ID,
     r1$summary.random$observation.locations$mean, pch=2)

--

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I try to do model selection under various logistic regression models by computing the marginal likelihood.
In the two  examples below, log mlik is 0.
Why is it so?
What would be the most reliable strategy for model selection in logistic regression?
Thanks.
G.

require(INLA)
nsites <- 200
Ntrials <- rep(20,nsites)
b <- rnorm(n=1)
f <- 1/( 1 + exp(-(b)))
z <- rbinom(n=nsites,size=Ntrials,prob=f)

res <- inla(formula=z~1,
            family="binomial",
            Ntrials=Ntrials,
            data = data.frame(z=z),
            control.data = list(link="logit",
              hyper = list(prec = list(prior="loggamma",param=c(0.1,0.1)))),
            control.fixed= list(prec.intercept = 1),
            control.compute = list(hyperpar=FALSE,return.marginals=FALSE,mlik=TRUE),
            control.inla=list(strategy = "laplace", npoints = 100))
res$mlik

y <- rnorm(nsites)
res <- inla(formula=z~1+y,
            family="binomial",
            Ntrials=Ntrials,
            data = data.frame(y=y,z=z),
            control.data = list(link="logit",
                 hyper = list(prec = list(prior="loggamma",param=c(0.1,0.1)))),
            control.fixed= list(prec.intercept = 1),
            control.compute = list(hyperpar=FALSE,return.marginals=FALSE,mlik=TRUE),
            control.inla=list(strategy = "laplace", npoints = 100))
res$mlik

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] marginal likelihood for logistic regression
messages.body_plain:
The marginal likelihood is defined as the normalisation constant for the
hyperparameters; see the INLA paper. In your exmaples there is no
hyperparameters, so another estimate is needed in that case.
Unfortunately, it is not yet implemented in that case, therefore it
returns 0.

For what it's worth, using pure marginal likelihood for this task is
fairly dangerous. Marginal likelihood is very sensitive to the choice
of priors placed on parameters which only exist under some models,
both "interesting" parameters and nuisance ones. This is in stark
contrast to estimation, which can be very robust to choice of priors.

small noise is always added when the linear predictor is constructed and
the behaviour is controled in 'control.predictor';
see ?control.predictor

the 'linear predictor' has one hyperparameter that has the following
(non-obvious) default values:

$theta
$theta$name
[1] "log precision"
attr(,"inla.read.only")
[1] FALSE

[1] "prec"
attr(,"inla.read.only")
[1] FALSE

$theta$initial
[1] 11
attr(,"inla.read.only")
[1] FALSE

$theta$fixed
[1] TRUE
attr(,"inla.read.only")
[1] FALSE

$theta$prior
[1] "loggamma"
attr(,"inla.read.only")
[1] FALSE

$theta$param
[1] 1e+00 1e-05
attr(,"inla.read.only")
[1] FALSE

$theta$to.theta
function (x)
log(x)
<environment: 0x63a71f0>
attr(,"inla.read.only")
[1] TRUE

$theta$from.theta
function (x)
exp(x)
<environment: 0x63a71f0>
attr(,"inla.read.only")
[1] TRUE

so the precision is default fixed and set to exp(11).

in most cases this is not something you want change or tune, unless
your're in a special case where the model is scaled very badly (but then
its better to rescale the data/model...).

if you have one unique component of an "iid" model added to each
component of the linear predictor, like

	y ~ ... + f(idx, model="iid") + ...

where idx=1:n, say, then you can instead make the fixed precision for
the noise in the linear predictor, random, by removing f(idx...),

	y ~ ... + ....

and then add

	inla(...., control.predictor = list(hyper = list(prec = list(fixed =
FALSE)))

or  using the old-style

	inla(..., control.predictor = list(fixed=FALSE)))

this will reduce the model-size, but I'm not sure its worth while,
really....

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: inla.finn
messages.body_plain:
Hi Cici,

This is a rather complicated question!

To begin with, almost everything you could ever need to know on this
topic is in Nick Higham's excellent (if rather daunting) book
"Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms" (in particular the
chapter on Cholesky decompositions).

So lets start at the beginning: You probably shouldn't be computing
the Cholesky factorisation of a semi-definite matrix.  While it's
"possible", it's very difficult for the obvious reason that Q+ E for
almost any E is no longer semidefinite, and so the operation is not
going to be stable in the presence of rounding error (even in the best
case, it can be catastrophically unstable).

More importantly, none of the operations make sense for sampling etc
for GMRFs unless L (and hence Q) is non-singular!  Adding a small
diagonal will "fix" this, it's almost certainly not what you want to
do - you either want to add a  "large" matrix in the form of
conditioning on data, or you want to condition on a system of linear
constraints (eg sum to zero constraints) that make the conditional
GMRF proper.  Rue (2001) always assumes that Q is a proper precision
matrix (and hence SPD), similarly in the book whenever an intrinsic
field is used, it is sampled etc conditional on linear constraints.

To the best of my knowledge, which is incomplete here, INLA does not
(by default) add a small number to the diagonal for stability. (You
can make it do this with the "diagonal" option in control.inla, but,
as above, you shouldn't).

The correct behaviour when you have a positive semi-definite matrix is
for it to either compute a singular L [if you're a) lucky and b) using
pivoting)] or to fail because it encountered a zero (or negative)
pivot.

Now, let's talk about truth, computing, and numerical linear algebra!
For the Cholesky triangle L that the computer gives you LL^T is NEVER
equal to Q.  Absolutely unequivocally never.  The best that you can
ever say is that ||Q - LL^T|| is small (there are classical bounds on
this that say that ||Q - LL^T|| <= c_n u ||A||, where c_n is a small
constant and u~1e-16 is the machine precision.   Note that this *does
not* say that the computed L is close to the true Cholesky factor of
Q.  In practice, this doesn't matter - it's rare that real problems
are so catastrophically ill conditioned that you can compute an answer
and it's really really wrong.

In practice, if you have a poorly conditioned matrix (specifically if
20n^{3/2}||Q||||Q^{-1}||u >1), then the Cholesky decomposition is not
guaranteed to be computable in finite arithmetic.  This is  what
happens when the Cholesky factorisation fails (assuming Q is SPSD!).
There is pretty much nothing that you can do about this, other than
use higher precision floating point arithmetic, which most of the time
isn't practical!  It's entirely possible that the semidefinite matrix
that you "made up" was too ill conditioned for chol.spam to be able to
compute anything with it.

I hope this helps.

Dan

a comment on the diagonal issue: if precision matrix Q is
singular/numerically singular, then adding a diagonal d to it

	Q' = Q + diag(d)

and then producing samples from it, has a clear interpretation.

consider the following model

	x ~ GMRF(Q)

with observations

	y | x ~ N(x, diag(d))

that are all zero, so y=0.  then x|y=0 has precision matrix Q' and mean
zero. so adding 'd' to the diagonal, just give you samples from x|y=0,
using the model above.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan,

ideally inla.cpo recomputes all CPO values for which result$cpo$failure > 0. That means it runs the usual inla-model stored in "result", say, and then checks for failures. For each idx with "result$cpo$failure[idx] > 0" inla is called again using the control.expert = list(cpo.manual = TRUE, cpo.idx = idx) option. Then, I assume that the idx-th observation is internally removed and the cpo-value is calculated from the marginal of linear predictor. To the best of my knowledge there is no scaling involved.

I tried the inla.cpo function out at two examples and also got always CPO values of 1 returned. Thus, I compared it with a "real" manual re-computation, where I remove the observation myself, run INLA and derive the CPO from the corresponding marginal of the linear predictor. Now, I get the expected low CPO values, see the code below. I am not sure what is going wrong in inla.cpo, but I will try to find it out.

Regards
Andrea

########################################################
library(INLA)

data(Germany)
## just make a duplicated column
Germany = cbind(Germany,region.struct=Germany$region)

g = system.file("demodata/germany.graph", package="INLA")

##Define the model
formula <- Y ~ f(region.struct, model="besag",graph.file=g) +
               f(region, model="iid") + x

## Run the model
result <- inla(formula,family="poisson",data=Germany,E=E,
    control.compute = list(cpo=TRUE))

## Find the position of failures
idx.failure <- which(result$cpo$failure > 0)

## Examplary, re-calculate the cpo for one of the failures
i <- idx.failure[3]
## Remove the observation for which we received the failure
y_tmp <- Germany$Y[i]
Germany$Y[i] <- NA

## Run INLA and return the marginals for the linear predictor
result2 <- inla(formula,family="poisson", data=Germany,E=E,
            control.inla = list(int.strategy = "grid", diff.logdens = 5),
            control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE))

## Set back the observation
Germany$Y[i] <- y_tmp
## Get the marginal for the linear predictor
eta.marginal <- result2$marginals.linear.predictor[[i]]
cpo.manual <- inla.emarginal(function(x, yy, EE) dpois(yy, lambda = EE*exp(x)),
                  eta.marginal, yy=Germany$Y[i], EE=Germany$E[i])

## Compare it with the result you get when using the internal option
## to calculate CPO's manually
result3 <- inla(formula,family="poisson", data=Germany,E=E,
        control.inla = list(int.strategy = "grid", diff.logdens = 5),
        control.expert=list(cpo.manual=TRUE, cpo.idx=i),
        control.mode=list(result=result, restart=TRUE))
cpo.inla.manual <- result3$cpo$cpo[i]

## Compare the different CPOs:
## standard INLA (with failure[i] > 0), manual re-computation, inla re-computation)
c(result$cpo$cpo[i], cpo.manual, cpo.inla.manual)
[1] 0.03567603 0.03488637 1.00000000

Dear all,

It looks like there's a problem with the iid2d model in the latest development version of INLA. Running the demo leads to a segfault: with the verbose option on, I get:

Store results in directory[/tmp/RtmpnI2tNQ/file7cba5c4cf7dd/results.files]
Segmentation fault

if I replace "iid2d" with "iid", the problem disappears. Here's the code I'm using, it's simply a copy-and-paste from the PDF:
n = 1000
N = 2*n
rho = 0.5
## set variances
Sigma = matrix(c(1/1, NA, NA, 1/2), 2, 2)
## and the correlation
Sigma[1,2] = Sigma[2,1] = rho*sqrt(Sigma[1,1]*Sigma[2,2])
## need it to simulate data
library(mvtnorm)
## first example
y = yy = rmvnorm(n, sigma=Sigma)
y = c(y[,1], y[,2])
i = 1:N
formula = y ~ f(i, model="iid2d", n=N)
r = inla(formula, data = data.frame(i,y),
control.data=list(initial=10,fixed=TRUE),verbose=T)

Best,

Simon Barthelmé
